title: CLEAR Travel Tips: What Do I Do If My Luggage is Lost
summary: Lost your luggage? Learn how to report and track a missing bag, save receipts, file a claim, and request reimbursement from your airline.
body_markdown:
Losing a bag at the airport can be stressful, especially when you’re ready to get on with your trip. If your luggage doesn’t arrive at baggage claim, knowing what to do next can make the situation easier to manage.


## **What Should You Do if Your Bag Is Missing at Baggage Claim?**


If your checked bag still hasn't appeared by the time the carousel stops, report the issue before leaving the airport.


First, check nearby carousels and the baggage area in case your suitcase was placed somewhere else. Then head to your airline's baggage service office, usually located near baggage claim.


Tell the airline your checked bag didn't arrive and ask to file a delayed or missing baggage report. The[U.S. Department of Transportation](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) recommends filing a baggage claim with your airline as soon as possible.


Before you leave, make sure you have your baggage report or reference number, baggage claim tag, and the airline's contact information. Keep a copy or confirmation of your report, and ask how you'll receive updates or how your bag will be delivered if it's found.


Make sure to hold on to your boarding pass and baggage tag—you may need them later.


‍


## **How Do You File a Delayed or Missing Bag Report with an Airline?**


Start with the airline that operated your flight. Visit its baggage service office at the airport and ask to file a report.


Some airlines also let you report missing baggage online or through their app. Follow your airline's instructions, since requirements can vary.


Provide as much information as you can about your flight and bag. Before you leave, ask for a reference or file number, which you can use to track your bag and contact the airline for updates.


The U.S. Department of Transportation recommends staying in close communication with the airline while it works to locate your bag.


‍


## **What Details Should You Provide to Help the Airline Locate Your Bag?**


The more accurately you can describe your suitcase, the easier it may be for airline staff to match it with a bag they've located.


Be ready to share your name and contact information, flight number, travel date, and baggage tag or claim number. Describe your bag's color, size, and brand, along with identifying details like straps, stickers, or luggage tags.


You may also need to provide your destination and an address where the airline can deliver your bag. The airline may ask for a general description of what you packed inside.


Photos can help, too. Before future trips, take a quick photo of your suitcase and what you've packed. If your bag goes missing, you'll have a visual reference ready.


‍


## **How Can You Track a Delayed Checked Bag With the Airline?**


Once you've filed a report, use the reference number from your airline to check your bag's status.


Many airlines offer baggage tracking through their website or mobile app. According to the[U.S. Department of Transportation](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , airlines use tracking tools to identify the location of missing checked bags, and some provide passengers with electronic baggage-location updates.


Keep an eye on the airline's tracking tool, along with your phone and email. If the status isn't changing or you have questions about delivery, use the baggage service contact information you received when you filed your report.


A personal luggage tracker can give you additional location information, but you'll still need to file a baggage report with your airline to get your bag returned and pursue reimbursement.


‍


## **What Documents Should You Keep for a Lost or Delayed Bag Claim?**


Keep your travel and baggage records until your bag has been returned and any claim or reimbursement is resolved.


That includes your boarding pass, baggage claim tag, flight itinerary, missing baggage report, and reference number. Keep photos of your suitcase if you have them, along with emails, messages, and other communication with the airline.


It's also helpful to make a list of what you packed and save proof of purchase for valuable items when available.


Most importantly, save itemized receipts for necessary purchases you make while your bag is delayed. If the bag is eventually declared lost, the airline may also ask for receipts or other proof of value for certain belongings.


‍


## **What Reimbursement Can You Get for Essentials During a Baggage Delay in the U.S.?**


If you're away from home without your checked bag, you may need to buy essentials like toiletries or clothing.


For domestic U.S. travel, airlines must compensate passengers for reasonable, verifiable, and actual incidental expenses caused by a baggage delay, up to applicable liability limits, according to the[U.S. Department of Transportation](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , which is why it's important to keep your receipts.


Buy what you reasonably need while you're separated from your bag and save the itemized receipts. What's considered reasonable can depend on your circumstances, so check your airline's baggage policy and ask what documentation it requires.


Basic toiletries and a change of clothes, for example, may qualify as reasonable purchases when you're away from home without your luggage. Keep purchases focused on what you need during the delay.


### **Which Receipts Qualify for Delayed Baggage Incidental Expense Reimbursement?**


Keep itemized receipts for reasonable and necessary purchases you make because you don't have access to your checked belongings.


Depending on your circumstances, that could include toiletries, basic clothing, or other essentials you need during the delay.


The U.S. Department of Transportation says airlines can't impose arbitrary daily reimbursement limits that prevent passengers from recovering reasonable, actual, and verifiable expenses up to the applicable baggage liability limit.


Itemized receipts provide clearer documentation than a credit card statement alone. Keep them with your baggage report and any records showing how long your bag was delayed.


If you're unsure whether a larger purchase will qualify, check with your airline first.


‍


## **When is a Delayed Bag Typically Declared Officially Lost by Airlines?**


There's no single timeline for every airline.


According to the[U.S. Department of Transportation](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) , most airlines declare a bag lost between five and 14 days after a flight, though individual policies can vary.


Until then, your bag will generally remain a delayed baggage case while the airline continues searching for it.


Stay in contact with your airline and follow its instructions. If the airline determines your bag is lost, you can move forward with a formal compensation claim.


‍


‍


## **How Do You Submit a Formal Claim if the Airline Declares Your Bag Lost?**


Reporting a missing bag and filing a formal lost baggage claim aren't always the same thing.


Once your airline declares your suitcase lost, follow its instructions for submitting a compensation claim. You'll typically need information from your original baggage report, including your reference number, boarding pass, flight information, and baggage claim tag.


The airline may also ask for a description of your suitcase and an inventory of what was inside. Include the approximate value of your belongings and receipts or other proof of purchase for valuable items when available.


For domestic U.S. flights, airlines may limit their liability for lost, damaged, or delayed baggage to $4,700 per passenger. Airlines can pay more but aren't required to, and reimbursement for a lost bag and its contents may account for depreciation.


Different liability limits apply to most international flights covered by the Montreal Convention. Check the U.S. Department of Transportation's[baggage guidance](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and your airline's policy for current international limits.


If your airline declares your bag lost, it's also required to refund the fee you paid to transport that bag.


‍


## **Can You Get Your Checked Bag Fee Refunded if Your Bag Is Delayed?**


Potentially, yes. Under current U.S. Department of Transportation rules, you're entitled to a refund of your checked baggage fee when your bag is lost or significantly delayed, subject to certain exceptions.


For domestic flights, a bag is significantly delayed if it isn't delivered within 12 hours after your flight arrives.


For qualifying international flights between a U.S. and foreign airport, the threshold is 15 hours when the flight is 12 hours or less and 30 hours when the flight lasts more than 12 hours.


You'll need to file a mishandled baggage report with the airline. Once that report is on file and the delay meets the applicable threshold, the baggage fee refund should be issued automatically, according to the[U.S. Department of Transportation](https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/aviation-consumer-protection/refunds?utm_source=chatgpt.com) . Some exceptions apply.


‍


## **How Do You File a DOT Complaint if the Airline Won't Resolve Baggage Issues?**


Start by giving the airline an opportunity to resolve your baggage claim. Keep copies of your report, receipts, claim forms, and communications so you have a record of what happened.


If you can't resolve the issue with the airline, you can submit an air travel service complaint to the U.S. Department of Transportation's Office of Aviation Consumer Protection.


Include the key details of your trip and baggage issue, along with relevant documentation. Explain what happened, what you've already done to resolve it with the airline, and what remains unresolved.


The U.S. Department of Transportation's[lost, delayed or damaged baggage guidance](https://www.transportation.gov/lost-delayed-or-damaged-baggage?utm_source=chatgpt.com) also explains airline responsibilities, baggage liability limits, and reimbursement requirements.


‍


## **Prepare Before You Fly**


You can't guarantee your checked bag will arrive with you, but a few simple habits can make a delay easier to manage.


Take a photo of your suitcase before checking it and keep your baggage claim tag until you've collected your bag. Put your name and current contact information on or inside your luggage.


Keep medications, travel documents, valuables, and anything you can't easily replace in your carry-on.


You can also use a personal luggage tracker for additional location information. Just remember that a tracker doesn't replace filing a missing baggage report with the airline if your bag doesn't arrive.


‍


## **Know What to Do When Your Bag Doesn't Arrive**


If your checked bag doesn't show up at baggage claim, your first move is simple: report it to your airline before you leave the airport.


Keep your baggage tag, report number, and receipts. Track your bag and stay in contact with the airline while it searches. If you need essentials during the delay, save itemized receipts for reasonable purchases. If your bag is eventually declared lost, follow your airline's process to file a formal claim.


Knowing what to do ahead of time can make an unexpected baggage problem easier to manage—so you can spend less time figuring out next steps and more time getting back to your trip.
